column2: When one fears no other and others fear him no more, when he neither desires nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
That craving which the foolish find hard to abandon, which does not age even as a man ages, which is a disease lasting until death — happy is he who gives it up.
As a man grows old, his hair grows old and his teeth grow old; but the hope of life and the hope of wealth do not grow old even in the aged.
Whatever pleasure of desire there is in this world, and whatever great heavenly bliss, is not worth a sixteenth part of the imperishable bliss of Krishna.
Having said this, the royal sage set out for the forest with his wife; the illustrious one performed austerities on Bhrigutunga and remained there.
Having kept the vow of the sages, he attained heaven from that very place. His five lineages are holy and honoured by the divine sages.
By them the whole earth is pervaded, as by the rays of the sun. A man who hears this becomes blessed, rich in offspring, long-lived and famous.
O best of the twice-born, by reading or hearing the whole account of Yayati —
It is heard, O best of sages, that this king duly performed seven hundred sacrifices in the seven continents.
All the sacrifices of that mighty-armed, supremely radiant king had golden altars and golden sacrificial posts.
They were adorned by all the illustrious gods standing in their aerial cars, and were ever graced by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Then the Gandharva Narada, beholding the deeds and greatness of that royal sage, sang a verse about that king:
Surely no men will attain the state of Kartavirya, whether by sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valour or learning.
Through his yogic power he was seen in all seven continents at once, with bow, sword and quiver, a king on his chariot with his retinue.
By the power of that great king nothing was ever lost; there was no distress and no confusion, and his subjects were protected by dharma.
For eighty-five thousand years that lord of men ruled as emperor and universal sovereign, possessor of all jewels.
He himself was the protector of cattle and the guardian of the fields; through his yoga Arjuna himself became Parjanya, the bringer of rain.
With his thousand arms hardened by the strokes of the bowstring, he shone like the autumn sun with its thousand rays.
That lord of men, with a thousand serpents, conquered the assembly of Karkotaka at Mahishmati and settled his city there.
The lotus-eyed king, sporting at ease in the rainy season, checked the rush of the ocean and made it seem like the season of rains.
Stirred by his sport, the Narmada, garlanded with golden wreaths, approached him fearfully, roaring with waves strewn with pearls.
Once with his thousand arms he plunged into the great ocean and, out of season, made it overflow its shores as if tossed by the wind.
When the great ocean was churned by his thousand arms, the great Asuras dwelling in Patala lay hidden and motionless.
The great waves were shattered, fish and great serpents hid, heaps of foam were tossed about, and unbearable whirlpools were hurled up.
The king agitated the ocean with his thousand arms, like the milk ocean churned by the gods and Asuras.
As when stirred by Mandara for the sake of the nectar, the great serpents, terrified at seeing that fearsome best of kings, suddenly fled.
The great serpents bowed their heads and became still, like plantain trees motionless in the windless evening.
Stringing his strong bow, with five hundred arrows he stunned Ravana, lord of Lanka, together with his army, by force.
Having conquered him and brought him under control, he bound him in Mahishmati. Then Pulastya went to Arjuna and conciliated him.
Entreated by Pulastya, the king released the descendant of Pulastya. The twang of the bowstrings of his thousand arms resounded
like the thunder of massed clouds bursting at the end of an age. Ah, how mighty in battle was the Bhargava who cut him down,
who in battle lopped off his thousand arms like a grove of golden palms! Once, Agni, being thirsty, begged alms of him.
The lord of the people gave Agni the seven continents as alms — cities, cattle stations, villages and towns everywhere.
Agni blazed in his arrows, eager to burn; and by the might of that lord of men the glorious fire
burned the mountains and forests of Kartavirya. That Haihaya, as fire, burned the entire empty hermitage of Varuna's son
with its groves and splendour — the excellent, radiant son whom Varuna had begotten long ago,
the sage named Vasishtha, also known as Apava. Then the mighty Apava in anger cursed Arjuna:

O Haihaya, since you did not spare this forest of mine, another will slay you for this dreadful deed.
brahmandpuran:107:46	You, the king named Arjuna, son of Kritavirya — the mighty Rama, best of warriors,
brahmandpuran:107:47	a powerful ascetic brahmin, will forcibly cut off your thousand arms, crush you and slay you.
So Rama became the death of that wise king through the curse; yet that king himself had formerly chosen this as a boon.
He had a hundred sons, of whom five were great chariot-warriors — skilled in arms, strong, heroic, righteous and famous:
Shura, Shurasena, Vrishasya and Vrisha, and Jayadhvaja, founder of a line and lord of the people in Avanti.
Jayadhvaja's son was the valiant Talajangha; his hundred sons are known as the Talajanghas.
Of these high-souled Haihayas five groups are famed: the Vitihotras, the Bhojas, the Avantis,
the valiant Tundikeras and the Talajanghas. Vitihotra's son was a king named Ananta.
His son was Durjaya, destroyer of foes. That king too had the power that nothing in his realm was ever lost.
By his power the great king protected his subjects; his wealth never perished, and whatever was lost he recovered.
Whoever recounts here the birth of the wise Kartavirya — his fortunes ever increase and his dharma grows.
As a sacrificer and as a giver, so is he honoured in heaven, O king.
Be born quickly — blessings on you! Why do you remain there? The girl in the womb replied to him, "If you give a cow every day,
then after three years I will come forth from the womb." Her father said, "So be it," and fulfilled her wish.
Her son is remembered as Akrura, son of Shvaphalka — generous, a sacrificer, a hero, learned, fond of guests and lavish in gifts.
Upamangu and Mangu, Mridura and Arimejaya, Girirakshas, then Yaksha, Shatrughna and Arimardana,
Dharmavriddha, Sukarman and also Gandhamada, Avaha and Prativaha, and the fair lady Vasudeva.
From Akrura and Augraseni were born two sons who delighted their family, Devavan and Upadeva, resembling gods.
The sons of Chitraka were Prithu and Viprithu, Ashvagriva and Ashvavaha, Suparshvaka and Gaveshana,
Arishtanemi, Ashvasya, Suvarman and Varmabhrit, Abhumi and Bahubhumi, and two daughters, Shravishtha and Shravana.
From Satyaka the daughter of Kashi obtained four sons: Kukura, Bhajamana, Shuchi and Kambalabarhisha.
Kukura's son was Vrishni; Vrishni's son was Kapotaroman, and his son was Viloman.
His son was the learned Andhaka, friend of Tumburu; his other names are said to be Chandanodakadundubhi.
His son was Abhijit, and from him was born Punarvasu. That best of men performed the horse sacrifice for the sake of a son.
In the midst of the Atiratra rite he rose up from the middle of the assembly: the learned Punarvasu, knower of dharma, generous and a sacrificer.
Then twins were born to Abhijit, it is said: Ahuka and Ahuki, renowned as foremost among the wise.
Here they cite these verses concerning Ahuka: "Of chariots with their attendants and banners, armoured,
thundering like clouds, he had ten thousand. He was never untruthful, never without sacrifice, never gave less than a thousand.
He was never impure, never unrighteous, never unlearned, never feeble." We have heard that Dhriti was the son of Ardraka.
With that retinue the peerless Ahuka went forth with eighty myriads of horses resembling young colts.
In the eastern quarter the Bhoja king had twenty-one thousand elephants with girths of silver and gold,
and as many thousands likewise in the northern quarter; bells, it is said, rang out for the Bhoja ruler.
Ahuka gave his sister Ahuki in marriage in Avanti. From Ahuka and the daughter of Kashi two sons were born,
Devaka and Ugrasena, both like children of the gods. To Devaka were born heroic sons like the thirty gods:
Devavan, Upadeva, Sudeva and Devarakshita. They had seven sisters, whom he gave to Vasudeva:
Dhritadeva, Upadeva, another named Devarakshita, Shridevi, Shantideva and Sahadeva,
and the seventh of them, the younger and lovely Devaki. Ugrasena had nine sons, of whom Kamsa was the eldest,
then Nyagrodha, Sunaman, Kanka, Shanku, Subhumi, Sutanu, Rashtrapala, Yuddhatushta and Tushtiman.
They had five sisters: Kamsa, Kamsavati, Sutanu, Rashtrapali and the fair Kanka.
Ugrasena, born of the Kukuras and with many offspring, has been described. One who remembers this line of the boundlessly mighty Kukuras
obtains a large family of his own and becomes rich in offspring. Bhajamana's son was Viduratha, foremost of chariot-warriors.
Viduratha's son was the hero Rajadhideva. To that hero were born very powerful sons:
Vata, Nivata, Shonita, Shvetavahana, Shami, Gadavarman, Nidanta and Shatrujit.
Shami's son was Pratikshatra; Pratikshatra's son was Svayambhoja, and from Svayambhoja was born Hridika.
Hridika had ten sons of dreadful prowess; Kritavarman was the eldest and Shatadhanvan the middle one,
Devabahu, Subahu, Bhishak, Shvetaratha, Sudanta, Adhidanta, Kanaka and Kanakodbhava.
Devabahu's learned son was Kambalabarhisha; his son was Asamaujas, and Susamaujas was also famous.
To the sonless Asamaujas were then given Suchandra, Vasurupa and Krishna; these are remembered as the Andhakas.
Whoever constantly recites this line of the Andhakas obtains a large family of his own; there is no doubt of this.
In Ashmaki he begot the hero Devamidhusha. From Shura and Marisha, a Bhoja woman, ten sons were born.
First was mighty-armed Vasudeva, called Anakadundubhi; when he was born a kettledrum sounded in heaven.
A mighty sound of drums arose in heaven, and a great shower of flowers fell on Shura's house.
In the whole world of men there was none equal to him in beauty; that foremost man had radiance like the moon.
Then Devabhaga was born, then Devashravas, Anadhrishti, Vrika, Nandana and Srinjaya,
Shyama, Shamika and Gandusha. Their sisters were fair ladies: Pritha, Shrutadeva, Shrutakirti, Shrutashravas
and Rajadhidevi — these five were mothers of heroes. Shura gave his daughter Pritha to Kuntibhoja.
Hence Pritha, daughter of Kuntibhoja, is remembered as Kunti. Pandu, chief of the Kuru heroes, took her as his wife.
Pritha then bore three sons, radiant as fire, peerless heroes in the world with prowess equal to Indra's.
Pritha bore Yudhishthira from Dharma, Vrikodara from the Wind, and Dhananjaya from Indra.
From Madravati, it is well known, the Ashvins begot Nakula and Sahadeva, endowed with beauty, strength and virtue.
To Shrutadeva was born the son of Vriddhasharman, the mighty hero Dantavakra, lord of the Karushas.
From the Kaikeya and Shrutakirti was born mighty Santardana, and likewise the powerful Chekitana and Brihatkshatra,
and the very mighty brothers Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti. From Shrutashravas was born Shishupala of Chedi,
son of the royal sage Damaghosha, famed for his manliness, who formerly was the ten-headed crusher of foes,
whose younger brother was Kumbhakarna, brother also of Vaishravana. Vasudeva had thirteen fair wives:
Pauravi Rohini, Madira and another, Bhadra, Vaishakhi, and Sunamni the fifth,
Sahadeva, Shantideva, Shrideva, Devarakshita, Dhritadeva, Upadeva and Devaki the seventh,
and Sugandha and Vanaraji, two other attendants. Rohini Pauravi was the younger sister of Bahlika.
She was the eldest and beloved wife of Anakadundubhi. The eldest bore the sons Rama, Sarana and Shatha,
Durdama, Damana, Shubhra, Pindaraka and Kushitaka, and a daughter named Chitra; Rohini bore these eight.
Two sons, Nishatha and Ulmuka, were born to Rama; also Parshvi, Parshvamardi, Shishu and Satyadhriti,
Mandabahya, Ramana, Giriraka and Giri, Shulkagulma, Atigulma and Daridrantaka.
Hear by name the other five daughters: Archishmati, Sunanda, Surasa, Suvacha
and Shatabala. These were the children of Sarana. Bhadrashva, Bhadragupti, Bhadravishta,
Bhadrabahu, Bhadraratha, Bhadrakalpa, Suparshvaka, Kirtiman and Rohitashva were the sons of Shatha.
Abhibhuta was Durmada's son; these are remembered as born in Rohini's family. Nanda, Upananda, Mitra, Kukshimitra, Bala,
Chitra, Upachitra, Kritaka, Tushti and Pushti — these sons of Madira were born of Vasudeva.
Upabimba, Bimba, Sattvadanta and Mahaujas — these four famous and mighty ones were Bhadra's sons.
In Vaishali Shauri begot the excellent son Kaushika. From Shauri and Devaki were born Sushena and Kirtiman,
Udarshi, Bhadrasena, Rijudaya the fifth and Bhadradeva the sixth; Kamsa killed them all.
Then, in that state, the long-lived one was born — Vishnu, lord of the worlds, Krishna, the primeval Prajapati.
After Krishna was born Subhadra of gentle speech; Krishna and Subhadra — so the daughter of the Vrishnis is again described.
From Partha and Subhadra was born the chariot-warrior Abhimanyu. Of Vasudeva's seven illustrious wives,
hear by name the heroic sons who were born. From Shura's son and Sahadeva were born sons headed by Purva.
Shantideva bore to Shauri Janastamba, upholder of the line; the great-souled Agavaha was born of Vrikadevi.
From Shrideva himself was born one named Mandaka; Devarakshita bore two sons, Upasanga and Vasu.
Thus he had ten sons, and Kamsa killed them too. Vijaya, Rochana, Vardhamana and Devala —
these great-souled sons were borne by Shishiravati. The seventh, Devaki, bore a son named Sunaman,
and the illustrious Gaveshana, a wonderful fighter in battle. Wandering in a forest grove near the city, O brahmins,
Shauri begot on a Vaishya woman the imperishable son Kaushika. Sugandhi and Vanaraji were Shauri's two consorts.
Pundra and Kapila were the two sons of Sugandhi. Of them Pundra became king and Kapila went to the forest.
From another woman was born to Vasudeva a mighty hero named Jara, a Nishada, the foremost bowman.
The illustrious son of Devabhaga was famous; the learned say that Devashravas was his offspring.
From Ashmaki, Anadhrishti obtained a famous son, Nivrittashatru, slayer of foes, and the mighty Shraddhadeva.
Shraddhadeva was born of a Nishada woman and became well known; the illustrious Ekalavya was raised by the Nishadas.
Pleased, Krishna gave two sons to the childless Gandusha: Charudeshna and Samba, skilled in arms and of auspicious marks.
Ranti and Rantipala were the two sons of Nandana. To the sonless Vrika the mighty Vasudeva
gave the heroic son Saumi, and Shauri gave Kaushika as well. Dhanus and Viraja were the two sons of Srinjaya.
Shyama was childless; Shamika went to the forest, and, despising the Bhoja kingship, attained the state of a royal sage.
Whoever, keeping his vows, reads this birth of Krishna, or causes a brahmin to hear it, attains great happiness.
The god of gods, of great splendour, Krishna the primeval Prajapati, the Lord Narayana, was born among men for his divine play.
Through the austerity of Vasudeva, the lotus-eyed one was born of Devaki, four-armed and endowed with divine beauty and splendour.
The manifest Lord, the yogin Krishna, took human form; that same Lord is both unmanifest and of manifest form.
Since Narayana made both the perishable and the imperishable, the god became Narayana and Hari, the eternal one.
He who of old made the primal Person, Prajapati, from the lotus, and who became the son of Aditi, the joy of the Yadavas,
was known as the god Vishnu, the younger brother of Indra, whom Aditi propitiated for the sake of a son,
for the slaying of the enemies of the gods — Daityas, Danavas and Rakshasas. Then, in the line of Yayati, of the wise Vasudeva,
a holy family in which Lord Narayana took birth: the oceans trembled and the mountains shook,
the sacred fires blazed up when Janardana was born; auspicious winds blew and the dust settled.
The heavenly lights shone more brightly when Janardana was born. The constellation was Abhijit, the night was called Jayanti,
and the hour was named Vijaya when Janardana was born — the unmanifest, eternal Krishna, Hari, the Lord Narayana.
So the Lord was born, bewildering creatures with his maya. The lord of the gods rained a shower of flowers from the sky,
and great sages with Gandharvas in thousands attended, praising Madhusudana with auspicious words.
Vasudeva, seeing his son Adhokshaja born that night, marked with the Shrivatsa on his chest and his own divine signs,
said to him, "Withdraw this form, O Lord. I am afraid of Kamsa, my dear; that is why I speak thus.
My elder sons of wondrous appearance were killed by him." Hearing Vasudeva's words, the Lord withdrew his form.
With his leave, the father carried him to the house of Nandagopa. He stayed in Ugrasena's house and then gave him to Yashoda.
Yashoda and Devaki had been pregnant at the same time; Yashoda was the wife of Nandagopa, lord of the cowherds.
On the very night that the Lord Krishna was born in the Vrishni clan, a daughter was born to Yashoda.
Guarding the newborn, the illustrious Vasudeva gave his son to Yashoda and took the girl himself.
Giving him to Nandagopa, he said, "Protect him. This son of yours will bring every blessing to the Yadavas.
This child of Devaki will take away my sorrows." Then Anakadundubhi reported to Ugrasena's son
that a girl with auspicious marks had been born. Kamsa did not know that his sister's son had been born.
Then the wicked one, pleased, let her go too, saying, "As she is your daughter, so is she mine, no doubt. I will not kill her, O mighty-armed one; let her go where she pleases."
That girl grew up there, honoured in the house of the Vrishnis; the goddess raised the goddess joyfully as her own child.
Krishna, born in this manner, they call Prajapati. The eleventh was born for the protection of Keshava.
The Yadavas will worship her with concentrated minds, for by her Krishna, the god of gods of divine form, was protected.
The sages said: Why did Kamsa, the Bhoja king, kill the infant sons of Vasudeva? Please explain this to us.
Suta said: Hear how the foolish Kamsa crushed all the sons of Anakadundubhi as soon as each was born,
how, out of fear, the mighty-armed Krishna was sent away at birth, and how Govinda, the Supreme Person, grew up among the cows.
At the wedding of Devaki and the wise Vasudeva, Kamsa, who was then crown prince, acted as charioteer.
Then a divine voice from someone unseen was heard in the sky, loud and witnessed by the world, naming Kamsa:
O Kamsa, the woman you are carrying in your chariot out of affection — her eighth child will be your death.
Hearing that voice, the foolish Kamsa was distressed; drawing his sword, he wanted to kill the young woman.
The mighty-armed, valiant Vasudeva, out of friendship and affection, spoke to Kamsa, son of Ugrasena:

No kshatriya should ever kill a woman. I have seen a way out of this, O joy of the Yadavas.
brahmandpuran:109:232	The eighth child born of her, O lord of the earth, I will give to you; then do with it as is fitting.
brahmandpuran:109:233	But do not act as you please now, O generous one. Or I will hand over all her children to you, one by one.
brahmandpuran:109:234	Thus, O best of men, this voice will not prove false. Addressed and conciliated in this way, he accepted the proposal.
Vasudeva, having received his wife, rejoiced; but the sinful, foolish Kamsa killed his sons.
The sages said: Who is this Vasudeva, and the famous Devaki? Who is this Nandagopa, and the illustrious Yashoda,
he who begot Vishnu, whom Vishnu called father, she who conceived him, and she who nursed and raised him?
Suta said: The man was Kashyapa and his beloved was Aditi. Kashyapa was a portion of Brahma, and Aditi of the Earth.
Nanda is known as Drona, and Yashoda was Dhara. Then the mighty-armed god, fulfilling Devaki's desires,
moved over the earth, having entered a human body, bewildering all beings through his yoga-maya, he whose self is yoga.
When dharma perished, Vishnu himself was born in the Vrishni clan, to establish dharma and destroy the Asuras.
Rukmini, princess of Vidarbha; Satya, daughter of Nagnajit; Satyabhama, daughter of Satrajit; Jambavati; Rohini;
Shaibya; and sixteen thousand other queens. The fourteen troops of Apsarases said to be in heaven
were deliberately chosen and sent here by the gods and Indra; they were born in royal palaces to be wives of Vasudeva.
These are the famous and illustrious wives of Vishvaksena. Pradyumna, Charudeshna, Sudeva, Sharabha,
Charu, Charubhadra, Bhadracharu and Charuvidya were born of Rukmini, and a daughter, Charumati.
Sanu, Bhanu, Aksha, Rohita, Mantravit, Jara, Andhaka, Tamrachakra, Saubhari and Jaredhara —
and four sisters of theirs were born of Garudadhvaja: Bhanu, Saubharika, Tamraparni and Jarandhara.
These are Satyabhama's children; hear now Jambavati's offspring: Bhadra, Bhadragupta, Bhadrachitra,
the famous Badhrabahu, a daughter Bhadravati, and the renowned Sambodhani — know these as Jambavati's children.
Sangramajit, Shatajit and Sahasrajit — these are declared the sons of Vishvaksena by Sudevi.
Vrika, Vrikashva, Vrikajit and the fair lady Vrijini, Mitrabahu and Sunitha were the offspring of Nagnajiti.
Know that there were thousands of such sons; a hundred thousand sons of Vasudeva are recorded,
and eighty thousand heroes skilled in battle. Thus the line of Janardana has been told to you as it truly is.
Brihati was the wife of Puru, as were Sumadhya and Sugati; she was the daughter of the great-souled Brihaduktha of the Shini line.
Her three famous sons, splendid in battle, were Ananda, Kanaka and Shveta, and a daughter, Shveta.
Agavaha's sons were Chitra and the hero Chitraratha; Chitrasena is also remembered as his son, and a daughter Chitravati.
Tumba and Tumbavarchas were the two sons born to Tumba. Upasanga's two sons were Vajrara and Kshipra.
Bhurindrasena and Bhuri were the two sons of Gaveshana. From Yudhishthira's daughter was born his son Sudhanus.
From Samba, the daughter of Kashi obtained five swift sons; these five heroes are declared to be gods of true nature.
The grandsons of the great-souled Yadavas numbered three crores — the whole family and all who remain within it.
Vishnu stands as their measure and their lord; gods and men abide by his command.
The mighty Asuras slain in the wars of gods and demons were born here among men and oppress humanity.
For their destruction, a hundred families of the great-souled Yadavas arose in the Yadava clan.
Thus the descent of the Vrishnis has been told, in brief and in detail; it should be recited by one who seeks the attainment of fame.
The vital wind entered, joined with the Supreme Self; dwelling in the body in five forms, it sustains and nourishes it.
Prana, Apana, Samana, Udana and Vyana: Prana moves about, strengthening the supreme self within.
Apana governs the lower body, Udana the upper half of the embodied one; Vyana is that by which one extends, and Samana abides in all the joints.
Then arises his contact with the elements, which become objects of the senses: earth, wind, space, water and light as the fifth.
Entering all the senses, they performed their respective functions. The body is said to be of earth, and the wind to be the life-breath.
The openings arise from space, secretions flow from water, light dwells in the eye; each is remembered by the name of its source.
Gathering the sense-objects, which are set in motion by his power — thus the one eternal Person creates all these.
How did Vishnu come to be a man in this mortal world? This is our doubt, O wise one, and this our great wonder.
How did he who is the goal of all who move take on a human body? We wish to hear the deeds of Vishnu in due order.
Vishnu, the god, is declared by the Vedas to be the supreme wonder. Tell us of the wondrous birth of Vishnu, O wise one.

Let this wonder that has been announced be told, for it brings happiness: the manifestation of the great-souled one famed for strength and valour. Here is described the nature of Vishnu, wondrous in his deeds.
Suta said: I shall tell you of the manifestation of the great-souled one —
how the Lord of great austerity came to be among men: because of the sin of killing Bhrigu's wife, and by Bhrigu's curse, among humans
he is born at the ends of the ages to accomplish the purposes of the gods. Hear from me as I describe that divine body of Vishnu.
When the dharma of the age is overturned and the times grow lax, the Lord is born here among men to re-establish dharma — by reason of Bhrigu's curse, brought about through the gods and Asuras.
The sages said: How did he incur that curse through the gods and Asuras? We wish to know how that conflict of gods and Asuras came about.
Suta said: Hear from me as I relate how the conflict of gods and Asuras happened.
Formerly the Daitya Hiranyakashipu ruled the three worlds; then in turn the kingdom over the three worlds was held by Bali.
There was close friendship between the gods and the Asuras; for ten full ages the world remained undisturbed.
Gods and Asuras alike abided by the command of those two. When Bali was bound, a very terrible quarrel arose.
Then there was a terrible, great and destructive conflict between gods and Asuras; many battles took place over the continents.
In this Varaha age twelve such wars are remembered, ending with that of Shanda and Amarka. Hear their names in brief as I describe them.
The first was Narasimha's, the second Vamana's, the third Varaha's, the fourth the churning of the nectar,
the fifth the very terrible war over Taraka, the sixth the Adibaka, the seventh is remembered as that of Tripura,
the eighth the Andhakara, the ninth the Dhvaja, the tenth the terrible war with Vritra, then the Halahala,
and the twelfth is remembered as the other terrible one, the Kolahala. The Daitya Hiranyakashipu was slain by Narasimha.
Bali was bound by Vamana when the three worlds were traversed. Hiranyaksha was slain in single combat, in a dispute over divinity —
he of great strength and great courage, never defeated in battle; that Daitya was split in two by the tusk of Varaha.
Prahlada was defeated by Indra in battle at the churning of the nectar. Virochana, son of Prahlada, ever intent on killing Indra,
was overpowered and slain by Indra himself in the war over Taraka. He who had obtained invulnerability from Bhava by special weapons and the like,
Jambha, was slain in the sixth by Vishnu, who had entered Indra. When the gods were unable to withstand the ungodly foe,
all the Danavas were slain at Tripura by the three-eyed Shiva. Then in the Andhakara war the Daityas, gods and Rakshasas —
they were conquered by gods and men together with the ancestors. Vritra and the Danavas assembled with him, all of them together,
were slain by great Indra, strengthened with Vishnu's help. In the Dhvaja war Maya, hidden and skilled in yoga, was slain by great Indra.
Viprachitti, the great younger brother, entered the banner-mark; and the Daityas and Danavas assembled all together —
Vrisha, surrounded by all the gods, conquered them in the Halahala war. In the Kolahala war Raji, surrounded by the gods, conquered all the Daityas.
At the concluding bath of the sacrifice, the gods conquered Shanda and Amarka. These are the twelve wars that took place between gods and Asuras,
destructive to gods and Asuras alike and inauspicious for creatures. King Hiranyakashipu reigned for a hundred million years,
and seventy-two hundred thousand more, and eighty thousand besides, as lord of the three worlds.
In succession King Bali again ruled for a hundred million years, and sixty thousand and thirty million more.
For as long as Bali held sovereignty, so long was Prahlada kept subdued along with the Asuras.
These three are famed as the Indras of the mighty Asuras; for ten ages, it is said, all this was under the Daityas.
Then Shukra cursed the kingdom for ten ages more; great Indra took from Bali the three worlds, now free from trouble.
When the three worlds were taken from Prahlada by the turning of time, the three worlds passed in due course to Indra, chastiser of Paka.
Then Sacrifice abandoned the Asuras and went over to the gods. When Sacrifice went to the gods, the Asuras said to Kavya:
Why has Sacrifice left our kingdom before our eyes and gone to the gods? We cannot stay now; let us enter Rasatala.
Thus addressed, the dejected Kavya consoled them with his words: "Do not fear; I will sustain you by my own power.
Rain, plants, essences, and whatever is best — let them all remain; only their evil lies with the gods.
For your sake I will provide all of it; it is upheld by me." Then the gods, seeing the Asuras sustained by the wise Kavya,
took counsel, anxious and eager for victory: "This Kavya is forcibly turning all this away from us.
Let us go at once, before he strengthens them; let us kill them by force and drive the survivors to Patala."
Then the gods, enraged, rushed at the Danavas and struck them; being slain, they fled to Kavya alone.
Then Kavya, seeing them swiftly pursued by the gods, protected the terrified sons of Diti from the gods.
Kavya, seeing the gods standing there, reflected on fate; then, having meditated and recalling past events, he said to them:

The three worlds were all conquered by Vamana in three strides; Bali was bound, Jambha killed and Virochana slain.
brahmandpuran:110:106	The great Asuras were killed by the gods in the twelve wars; most of your leaders were slain by one means or another.
brahmandpuran:110:107	Only a few of you remain, and you are weak in battle. I will devise a policy for you; wait for some time.
brahmandpuran:110:108	I will go to Mahadeva for mantras and for victory. The priest will strengthen the fire, and with mantras it will burn them.
brahmandpuran:110:109	I will go to the blue-throated, red-hued god for mantras; after returning here I will favour you again.
brahmandpuran:110:110	Meanwhile practise austerities in the forest, clothed in bark; the gods will not harm you until I return.
brahmandpuran:110:111	Having obtained irresistible mantras from the great lord Maheshvara, we shall fight the gods again, and then you will win victory.
Having agreed among themselves, the Asuras said to the gods: "We have all laid down our weapons; you may range over the worlds.
We shall practise austerities in the forest, clothed in bark." Hearing Prahlada's words, spoken truthfully,
the gods turned back, relieved and joyful; since the Daityas had laid down their arms, they returned to their own abodes.
Then Kavya said to them: "Wait for some time, free of anxiety and devoted to austerity; time accomplishes one's purpose.
O Danavas, wait in my father's hermitage." Having instructed the Asuras, Kavya went to Mahadeva for refuge,
and bowing, he spoke to the Lord, the source of the world: "O god, I desire mantras that are not known to Brihaspati,
for the defeat of the gods and to give safety to the Asuras." Thus addressed, the god said: "You desire mantras, O brahmin?
Then keep the vow I prescribe, as a celibate with a concentrated mind: for a full thousand years, head downward, drink the smoke of the fire-pit.
If you drink it, blessings on you, you will obtain the mantras from me." So instructed by the god of gods, the great ascetic Shukra
touched the god's feet and said, "Very well. I will keep the vow, O god, as you have instructed me, O Lord."
Then he was appointed by the god to hold the pit and inhale its smoke. When Shukra had gone thus for the welfare of the Asuras,
he dwelt there with Maheshvara, practising celibacy for the sake of the mantras. Learning this, and that the Asuras had laid down their kingdom as a matter of policy,
the gods, seizing on that weakness in their anger, rushed upon them, all with weapons raised, led by Brihaspati.
Seeing the gods with weapons raised again, the hosts of Asuras sprang up suddenly, all of them terrified.

Though our weapons are laid down, though safety was granted, and though our teacher is keeping his vow, the gods have broken the compact and seek to kill their rivals.
brahmandpuran:110:127	Without our teacher, trusting and devoted to austerity, wearing rags, bark and skins, inactive and without possessions,
brahmandpuran:110:128	we can by no means defeat the gods in battle. Without fighting, let us take refuge with Kavya's mother.
Then in fear they took refuge with her, and she granted safety to those terrified Daityas who sought protection.
Seeing the Asuras sheltered by her, the gods, after weighing their strength and weakness, attacked them forcibly.
Then, seeing the Asuras being slain by the gods, the goddess grew angry and said, "I will make you Indra-less."
In her fury she quickly paralysed Indra and overpowered him. Seeing Indra paralysed, the gods, as if stupefied,
fled in fear on seeing Indra brought under her control. When the hosts of gods had gone, Vishnu said to Indra:
Enter into me — blessings on you — I will carry you away, O lord of the gods. So addressed, Purandara entered Vishnu.
Seeing him protected by Vishnu, the goddess angrily said, "O Maghavan, I will forcibly burn you together with Vishnu.
Let all beings witness the power of my austerity." Overpowered by her, the two gods Indra and Vishnu spoke together.
How can we both be freed? Vishnu said to Indra. Indra said, "Kill her, O Lord, before she burns us.
I am especially overpowered; kill her without delay." Then Vishnu, considering her, resolved to commit the killing of a woman.
Thinking of Indra in his plight, the Lord, the swift-acting slayer of Mura, acted quickly against her as she hastened.
Then the god Vishnu, understanding the cruel deed she intended, in anger hurled his weapon and Madhava cut off her head.
Seeing that dreadful killing of a woman, the lord Bhrigu was enraged; and Vishnu was cursed by Bhrigu for the slaying of his wife:
Since you, knowing dharma, have killed a woman who should not be killed, you shall be born seven times among men.
